prediction_scored: hit on the registered condition: the lower 95% bound, 3.21, is far above 0.2. Partial on magnitude: the estimate 4.55 is above the registered range of 0.5 to 3, which suggests that same-day common shocks or late closing of incidents on busy days inflate it; the previous day's hospital time, which these cannot affect in the same way, gives 1.06 (0.13 to 1.99).
settle: Hospital-level offload times (arrival to transfer of care) by day, from the FDNY or the state, joined to waits in each hospital's catchment; or a natural experiment such as a hospital's offload-team start date or a state offload standard.

notes: Primary elasticity 4.55 (3.21 to 5.88); call-count elasticity 5.28 (4.95 to 5.61). Previous-day turnaround 1.06 (0.13 to 1.99). Life-threatening calls (severity 1-3) 2.11 (0.95 to 3.27); other calls 4.94 (3.53 to 6.35). Annual means (all calls; wait = creation to first assignment, travel, time at hospital, seconds; calls per day): 2019 wait 100, travel 536, hospital 2168, calls 4201; 2022 101, 516, 2291, 4338; 2025 329, 649, 2437, 4417; 2026 to September 630, 722, 2517, 4412. From 2019 to 2025 log mean wait rose by 1.19 (a factor of 3.3); hospital time rose 12% and calls 5%. Applied to the annual changes, the same-day elasticities attribute 0.53 log points to hospital time and 0.27 to calls, about two thirds of the rise; with the previous-day elasticity hospital time accounts for 0.12. This extrapolation from daily variation to the trend is secondary and exploratory in strength. In 2026 wait almost doubled again while hospital time rose 3% and calls did not rise; the MMR attributes the year to a 5% fall in ambulance in-service hours (8,572 to 8,109 a day) and 11 hospital ambulances leaving the 911 system. Units in service are not in the open data, so staffing could not enter the model; year-month effects absorb it only as slow change. The MMR annual figures were read before registration; the daily data were not.
notes_referee: Referee reproduced 4.54 (3.20 to 5.88); year-week FE 3.49 (2.22 to 4.75). Verdict stands under rule 1. Placebo fails: next-day turnaround predicts today's wait at 2.40 (1.20 to 3.60); with year-week FE lag and lead near zero; afternoon turnaround predicts same morning's wait. Not evidence that offload time is a lever.
